assessment.nobel_worthiness: DMFT is the standard nonperturbative framework for strongly correlated electrons; it exactly maps the lattice problem onto a self-consistent impurity problem in infinite dimensions and underlies the Mott transition picture and, via DFT+DMFT, quantitative modelling of real correlated materials. Originality, clarity and decades of lasting impact across methods and materials are all strong from an electronic-structure perspective.
assessment.attribution: Vollhardt (with Metzner) opened the infinite-dimension limit, Georges and Kotliar built the self-consistent impurity mapping, and Kotliar extended it to realistic materials. The supplied three names cover the core, but the credit to Metzner and Müller-Hartmann is not on the list and some credit tension remains.
assessment.maturity: Over three decades of independent use, with benchmarks against experiment and cold-atom simulation; the interpretation is stable. Recognition is timely, arguably overdue.
uncertainties: Absence of other early contributors in the credited set (e.g. Metzner, Müller-Hartmann) complicates a fair three-person split.
DMFT is a method and framework rather than a single discovery, so the prize framing must be chosen carefully; I rely on my own knowledge of the history.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Predicting the quantum spin Hall state and Z2 topological insulators, and observing edge transport in HgTe wells, opened a whole class of topologically protected electronic phases and reshaped band theory and materials search. The work is conceptually original, clean, and extremely influential.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele made the decisive theoretical contribution (Z2 invariant); Molenkamp's group, with Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang prediction and König et al. observation, gave the experimental demonstration. Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang and 3D-TI contributors (Fu, Hsieh, Hasan) are not in the credited names, so credit is incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Independent confirmations in HgTe, Bi-Sb, Bi2Se3 and many materials, with ARPES and transport; very mature, and the Nobel 2016 topological prize left this strand unrecognised.
uncertainties: Many contributors beyond these three (Bernevig, Zhang, Fu, Hasan) complicate attribution.
Spillover with the 2016 topological-phases prize may be argued either way.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The magic-angle flat band prediction and the discovery of correlated insulators and superconductivity in twisted bilayer graphene created moire quantum materials as a tunable platform for correlated physics; strong originality and enormous follow-on activity, with a tight theory-experiment link.
assessment.attribution: Bistritzer and MacDonald made the flat-band prediction; Jarillo-Herrero's group made the decisive 2018 observations. The triple is natural, although Cao and Cory Dean's group and other experimentalists also made important contributions.
assessment.maturity: Roughly eight years old but extensively reproduced; microscopic origin of superconductivity and the correlated states is still debated, so some interpretive parts are unsettled. Recognition is somewhat early but plausible.
uncertainties: Mechanism of superconductivity and the nature of the correlated insulators remain contested.
Credit to other experimental groups and to Santos, Suarez Morell and others for earlier theory is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Room-temperature tunnel magnetoresistance in magnetic tunnel junctions, and then the coherent-tunnelling MgO junctions, enabled read heads and MRAM, and are a natural successor to the 2007 GMR prize in spintronics. Technological and scientific impact are both large and well demonstrated.
assessment.attribution: Miyazaki and Moodera reported room-temperature TMR in 1995; Parkin (and Yuasa) achieved the giant MgO-based values. Yuasa, Djayaprawira and the Julliere precursor and theory (Butler, Mathon) are not all in the credited names, so credit allocation is delicate.
assessment.maturity: Fully mature, with decades of device use and independent confirmation; timely or overdue.
uncertainties: MgO-barrier giant TMR contributions (Yuasa, Parkin, Butler) are only partly in the credited set.
Overlap with the earlier GMR prize may weigh against novelty for some members.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical-lattice quantum simulation realised Hubbard-type models with controllable parameters, including the superfluid to Mott insulator transition, and now provides a testbed for correlated many-body physics relevant to the problems I study in solids. Highly influential and conceptually clear.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and colleagues proposed the Hubbard realisation; Greiner (with Hänsch and Bloch) observed the Mott transition; Bloch built the quantum gas microscope era with Greiner. I choose three, leaving out Cirac and Dalibard, which is a real compromise.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally mature and widely replicated; the prize area is partially adjacent to 2001 and 2012 recognitions, so overlap with earlier prizes must be handled.
uncertainties: Five credited names with no clean three-person subset; leaving out Cirac, Dalibard and others is contestable.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Altermagnetism identifies a third collinear magnetic class with compensated moments yet spin-split bands, a genuine conceptual advance directly within magnetism and electronic structure theory, with promise for spintronics. Its originality is high, and symmetry arguments make the picture clean.
assessment.attribution: Šmejkal, Sinova and Jungwirth formulated the classification and predictions; earlier related work (Hayami, Yuan and others) and the experimental groups using ARPES and XMCD in MnTe, CrSb are not credited. The three names capture the main theoretical push.
assessment.maturity: The field is young; ARPES and other experiments on MnTe and CrSb support the spin splitting, but the breadth of device-relevant consequences is still being established. Likely premature compared with the other choices.
uncertainties: Premature: independent confirmation is recent and sample quality varies.
Priority questions with parallel theoretical work (Hayami, Yuan, Mazin) are unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Spin-transfer torque, predicted by Berger and Slonczewski and demonstrated in nanopillars, is a direct route to current-driven magnetic switching, with real impact on MRAM and on atomistic magnetisation dynamics. Technologically significant and conceptually elegant.
assessment.attribution: Berger and Slonczewski made the theoretical prediction, and Slonczewski is not among the credited names; Buhrman and Ralph delivered the decisive experimental demonstration. Berger is deceased, which constrains eligibility, so any workable configuration would be awkward.
assessment.maturity: Mature, with decades of devices and confirmation by multiple groups. Recognition is timely, but the attribution problem weighs heavily.
uncertainties: Slonczewski is missing from the credited names and Berger is deceased, so a clean laureate set is hard to form.
Other experimental groups (e.g. Tsoi, Katine) also contributed.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Quantum key distribution based on BB84 and Ekert's entanglement protocol connected foundations of quantum mechanics to a practical secure-communication technology; original, clear and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Bennett and Brassard authored BB84 and Ekert the entanglement-based protocol, so the supplied trio is natural and supportable, although the order and shares of credit are debatable and Wiesner's earlier ideas are outside the list.
assessment.maturity: Experimentally verified in fibre and satellite links, with commercial systems, though practical security loopholes persist and this is not my own field.
uncertainties: Practical security and deployment questions do not affect the principle but temper the technology claim.
Wiesner's earlier conjugate coding idea and the 2022 entanglement prize overlap are open issues.
